issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of title and possession must establish its own title, rather than relying on weaknesses in the opposing party’s title.
material_facts: The housing society sought a declaration of title and recovery of possession over the disputed land.
The society relied on its predecessors’ title and its own purchase, but the registered family settlement and partition deed did not mention the disputed land.
The society did not provide an acceptable explanation for the omission, and the lower courts focused substantially on the evidentiary value of the government’s land-register entries.
issues.conclusion: The society failed to establish its own title and possession, so the declaration and related relief could not stand; the appeal was allowed and the lower courts’ judgments were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit for declaration of title and possession, the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of its own title, irrespective of whether the defendant proves its competing claim. The Court relied on Maran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Thukalan Paulo Avira, AIR 1959 SC 31, and Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, (1995) 3 SCC 426.

predicates.title_declaration_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of title and possession of property.
predicates.claimant_title_document_omits_disputed_p: The document relied on to establish the claimant’s title did not identify or include the disputed property.
predicates.no_acceptable_explanation_for_omission: The claimant did not provide an acceptable explanation for the omission of the disputed property from the title document.
predicates.claimant_does_not_independently_establis: The claimant failed to establish title through evidence independent of the evidence that was insufficient to prove title.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks a declaration of title and possession, omits the property from a relied-on title document without an acceptable explanation, and otherwise fails to establish its own title, the title and possession relief is denied.

issues.legal_issue: Entries in revenue records or a record of rights, and the conferment of patta, do not by themselves establish title to property.
material_facts: The society relied on settlement and revenue records showing its predecessors as pattadars of the relevant survey land.
The society also relied on survey and revenue entries as evidence of its predecessors’ ownership.
The Court found that those entries did not independently establish title and that the society had to prove its predecessors’ title and the identity of the property conveyed to it.
issues.conclusion: The revenue and settlement entries, even if they carry evidentiary value, did not by themselves confer or establish title to the disputed land.
issues.legal_principle: Revenue records are not documents of title, entries in jamabandi do not prove title, and entries in revenue papers cannot by themselves form the basis for a declaration of title. A patta also does not itself confer title. The Court relied on Corporation of the City of Bangalore v. M. Papaiah, (1989) 3 SCC 612; Guru Amarjit Singh v. Rattan Chand, (1993) 4 SCC 349; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Keshav Ram, (1996) 11 SCC 257; Syndicate Bank v. Estate Officer & Manager, APIIC Ltd., (2007) 8 SCC 361; and Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu, 1991 Supp (2) SCC 228.

predicates.title_declaration_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of title and possession of property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_revenue_or_settlement: The claimant relied on entries in revenue, settlement, or record-of-rights documents to support its claim of ownership.

issues.definition: In a suit for a declaration of title and possession, relying on revenue or settlement entries as proof of title does not, by itself, establish title.
